- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
# On Arriving Late to Everything

Look up on a clear night and you are seeing things that may no longer exist. The light from some stars left them thousands of years ago. Others left so long ago that the stars themselves have since changed or died, and their light is still crossing the dark, arriving on schedule as if nothing had happened. When you see a star, you are receiving a letter that was written before the writer's death.

I find this comforting more than melancholy. Nothing we perceive is quite *now*. Light takes time to travel, and so do signals from your eyes to your brain. Your visual system takes tens of milliseconds to process what reaches it, which means the world you experience is always a little behind the world itself. Your brain covers the gap by predicting, smoothing, and filling in, so you rarely notice. You live in a slightly edited version of the present, assembled from messages that have already aged.

Sound works the same way. If you're across a large room from someone speaking, you hear them a few milliseconds after their lips move. At a football stadium, the crowd's roar reaches you after the goal is already visible. Every conversation is a small act of arriving late and deciding to act as if you were on time.

What strikes me is that this lateness isn't a flaw in the system. It's the only way a finite creature could perceive anything at all. Information needs time to cross distances, and a mind needs time to make sense of it. Even perfect perception would be delayed by the speed of light. The universe doesn't hand out the present; it hands out the recent past, and we are left to infer the rest.

There's something generous in that. Every act of understanding involves reaching across a gap: between a star and its light, a sentence and its meaning, a person's inner life and the words they can manage to say. Those gaps don't make connection impossible. They make it an act of interpretation, which is a kind of faith that the signal, delayed as it is, still carries something true.

So when I look up and see a star that might be gone, I try to remember that I'm not missing the present. The present, for any of us, was always a little out of reach. What we get instead is a steady arrival of messages from the past, and the strange privilege of deciding what they mean.
---
